publications.title: Strategic ligand design for modulating axial sites in dirhodium catalysts: towards enhanced asymmetric cyclopropanation
publications.description: In this work, we demonstrate a proof of concept that introducing a “fifth” ligand into a conventional bridging-ligand-modified Rh₂ catalyst system can enhance asymmetric cyclopropanation. This work highlights a new strategy for tuning the reactivity and selectivity of dirhodium catalysts and opens exciting possibilities for future catalyst design.

publications.title: Selective Sensing of Nerve Agent Simulant via Dirhodium(II,II) Paddlewheel Complexes Featuring Pendant Hemilabile Thioether Ligands
publications.description: This follow-up study on the untethered rhodium-NLB systems improves the selectivity of rhodium-based probes by introducing thioether ligands tethered to dirhodium complexes. The resulting systems more effectively distinguish between organophosphate simulants in the same G-series, DCP and DCNP, and chemically similar interferents, acetyl chloride, advancing molecular sensing strategies. Combining synthetic chemistry, spectroscopic characterization, and analytical evaluation, including UV-visible studies, mass spectrometry, solubility and stability testing, and interference analysis, this work offers a comprehensive approach that advances our ability to detect and differentiate DCP.

publications.title: Op-Ed “How federal research funding transformed my path.“ by Ernest Bennin
publications.description: In this op-ed, I share how federal funding transformed my academic path and enabled me to pursue advanced research in catalysis and molecular sensing.

publications.title: Chromogenic detection of the organophosphate nerve agent simulant DCP mediated by rhodium(II,II)paddlewheel complexes.
publications.description: This study uses nitrogenous Lewis bases (NLBs) and rhodium paddlewheel complexes to design a chemical probe for detecting diethyl chlorophosphate (DCP), a simulant of G‑series nerve agents. Combining synthetic chemistry, spectroscopic characterization, and analytical evaluation, including UV-visible studies, mass spectrometry, solubility and stability testing, and interference analysis, this work offers a comprehensive approach that advances our ability to detect and differentiate DCP.

publications.title: Heavy Metal Pollution Studies of Soil from the Oti-Dompoase Dumpsite in Kumasi. Fine Chemical Engineering
publications.description: This article investigates how soil at the Oti‑Dompoase dumpsite in Kumasi is contaminated by heavy metals associated with waste disposal, using field sampling and laboratory analysis to quantify pollution levels and potential risks. It evaluates the concentrations of key metals in surface soils and assesses their environmental impact, providing data that can inform monitoring and remediation efforts around the landfill area

aboutLong:
Ernest Bennin is a Ph.D. candidate at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville. He holds a Bachelor of Science degree in Chemistry from the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), Ghana. He is an NSF Center for Computer-Assisted Synthesis (NSF-CCAS) trainee, a member of the American Chemical Society (ACS), and NOBCChE. His current research focuses on:

Novel ligand designs (organic synthesis) | Rhodium paddlewheel complex synthesis | Utilization of rhodium paddlewheel complexes in asymmetric catalysis | Development of Rh(II)-based chemical sensors for chromogenic detection of biomolecules.
aboutShort: Ernest Bennin is a doctoral candidate in chemistry at the University of Tennessee-Knoxville, exploring research at the intersection of ligand design, synthesis, asymmetric catalysis, and chemical probes for poisonous substance detection.

news.title: President & Founding Member of GSA | UTK
news.description:
As a founding member and the elected president of the Ghana Student Association at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, I lead the development of the organization’s vision, governance structure, and long-term strategic direction. Elected by the founding members, I have played a central role in establishing a sustainable platform that promotes cultural awareness, community engagement, and academic support for Ghanaian students and the broader campus community.
Through intentional leadership and collaboration, I continue to strengthen the association’s institutional presence while fostering meaningful connections that celebrate heritage, encourage mentorship, and enhance cross-cultural dialogue across campus.

In this role, I lead strategic initiatives focused on professional development, industry engagement, and research exposure for undergraduate and graduate students in STEM. My presidency emphasizes building strong institutional partnerships, expanding mentorship opportunities, and creating platforms that connect members to real-world scientific innovation. Through collaborative leadership, I work to strengthen the chapter’s impact both on campus and within the broader scientific community.

news.title: NOBCChE 2025 Conference | Atlanta, GA
news.description:
In 2025, my abstract “Chromogenic Detection of the Organophosphorus Nerve Agent Simulant DCP Mediated by Rhodium(II,II) Paddlewheel Complexes" was accepted for presentation, and the Advancing Science Conference Grant was awarded.
This conference was truly motivating to share recent progress on Rh(II,II)-based chemical sensors for OPNA detection and to engage in inspiring conversations with researchers and professionals passionate about driving chemical innovation.
It was also an honor, in my role as president of NOBCChE-UTK, to meet with distinguished leaders such as Dr. Arthur W. Martin and LaRico Treadwell, Ph.D., to discuss both our challenges and the exciting events ahead.

news.title: NOBCChE 2024 Conference | Orlando, FL
news.description: In 2024, my abstract “Asymmetric Cyclopropanation on Dirhodium(II,II) Paddlewheel Complexes with Tethered, Axially Coordinated Ligands” was selected for presentation at the NOBCChE 2024 51st conference (“Building Momentum”). The event provided valuable opportunities to engage with experts sharing cutting-edge research; reconnect with KNUST alumni, peers from other institutions, NOBCChE leaders, and professionals from AbbVie, Merck, DuPont, Waters, and beyond; and foster personal and professional growth.

news.description: My Ph.D. research is part of a collaborative project supported by the NSF C-CAS program. This visit provided hands-on training in building, optimizing, and analyzing dirhodium paddlewheel complexes using density functional theory (DFT). I was trained by Dr. Ryan O’Connell (then a Ph.D. researcher in Prof. Olaf Wiest’s group), and this collaboration has continued beyond the visit. During my stay, I also presented my research, emphasizing the role of DFT calculations in providing selectivity insight to guide catalyst design.

news.title: The Graduate Student Senate Travel Award | UTK

news.title: Joined NSF-CCAS
news.description: In 2023, with the support of my principal investigator, I joined the NSF Center for Computer-Assisted Synthesis (C-CAS), a multi-institutional network that brings together synthetic chemists, computational chemists, computer scientists, and industry partners to accelerate reaction discovery and improve sustainable synthesis. The cross-disciplinary exposure I have gained through C-CAS has been invaluable in advancing my efforts to develop more selective and efficient catalysts for asymmetric synthesis.

news.title: Darko Research Group | UTK
news.description:
In January 2023, I officially joined the Darko Research Group after successfully completing a synthetic assignment, my first time independently carrying out a full synthesis, given my primarily analytical background. My PI designed this task to assess my potential in a lab that focuses largely on organic and inorganic chemistry, with some analytical instrumentation, and it marked a key turning point in my transition toward synthesis‑driven research.
Moreover, I met Eric Fussel and Desiree Moore, who were fourth-year Ph.D. students. They were very helpful and made the lab environment welcoming, which made my transition much easier.

news.title: FY23 Grad School Fellowship | University of Tennessee
news.description: In 2022, I received the FY23 Graduate School Fellowship at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, to pursue my Ph.D. in chemistry directly after completing my bachelor’s degree. This five‑year award provides sustained support for my graduate studies and research, allowing me to transition seamlessly from undergraduate training into a full‑time research-focused doctoral program. Being selected for this fellowship has affirmed my potential as an emerging scientist and given me the resources and flexibility to focus on impactful, long-term research goals.

This semester I taught General Chemistry (CHEM 123) with a combined class size of 48. Wrapping up a memorable semester with an amazing group of students. Their enthusiasm, questions, and dedication made teaching truly enjoyable. Moments like these remind me why I’m passionate about education and mentorship

projects.title: Original Research Proposal Examination | Chemistry, UTK
projects.description:
In November 2025, I successfully passed my O.R.P. (Original Research Proposal) examination, a major doctoral milestone in the Department of Chemistry at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville. This rigorous fourth-year assessment requires Ph.D. candidates to develop and defend a 15-page original research proposal unrelated to their dissertation work. The proposal is evaluated through an oral defense before a faculty committee and serves as a decisive pass-or-fail examination. Unsuccessful performance results in completion of the program with a master’s degree.

My proposal focused on the design and application of oxovanadium complexes as molecular probes for the detection of Plasmodium falciparum, introducing a novel strategy to distinguish between active and inactive malaria infections. This approach addresses a longstanding diagnostic limitation in global health, where current methods often struggle to differentiate persistent parasitic markers from ongoing infection. The project demonstrated my ability to conceptualize independent, interdisciplinary research at the interface of inorganic chemistry and biomedical diagnostics.

projects.title: 3rd Year Seminar | Chemistry | UTK
projects.description: As part of the Ph.D. program at the University of Tennessee, students are required to present a departmental seminar based on their second-year research proposal. This presentation highlights research progress, challenges encountered, strategies for overcoming those challenges, and any new directions or emerging projects stemming from the original proposal. It also serves as an opportunity to share personal and professional milestones with the department, including grants, awards, conference participation, honors, and public features.

projects.title: Mentorship | Chemistry | UTK
projects.description: I had the opportunity to mentor Taylor Nicole Totorp, providing her with hands-on experience in essential laboratory techniques such as maintaining a lab notebook, setting up chemical reactions, performing purification processes (including chromatography and liquid–liquid extraction), and analyzing data using NMR spectroscopy. Additionally, I guided her in developing key soft skills, including scientific communication through poster and group meeting presentations, as well as scientific document preparation.

In 2024, as part of the UTK Chemistry PhD program, I passed the comprehensive qualifying exam (requiring a minimum GPA of 3.0/4.0) to advance. My presentation focused on ligand-modified dirhodium complexes for asymmetric cyclopropanation and OPNA simulant detection, building on prior reports by incorporating dansyl fluorophores to enhance sensitivity. This rigorous training tested core chemistry concepts, scientific communication, and broader research impacts.

projects.title: Chemistry Debate Judge | Chemistry Department | KNUST

Kwansah, Prof. Osei-Akoto, and Prof. Darko, on both teaching and laboratory activities. projects.title: Ernest Bennin | B.S in Chemistry
projects.description: I earned my Bachelor of Science in Chemistry (first class honors; GPA 3.69/4.00) from the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), where I built a strong foundation in organic, inorganic, physical, and analytical chemistry and gained extensive hands-on laboratory experience. My undergraduate work focused on environmental chemistry. As an open‑minded young chemist, I was less concerned with specializing early than with contributing to science and improving lives, so I remained open to wherever my academic path might lead. This mindset continues to shape my current research interests and long‑term professional goals

projects.title: Undergraduate project | KNUST
projects.description: As part of my final‑year undergraduate project in the Department of Chemistry at KNUST, I investigated the quality of groundwater used for drinking in the Offinso‑North District of the Ashanti Region of Ghana under the supervision of Prof. Nkansah A. Asantewaah. The study focused on measuring key physicochemical parameters such as pH, electrical conductivity, total dissolved solids, alkalinity, hardness, and turbidity and the levels of selected metals and nutrients in borehole water. Ten borehole samples from different communities were analyzed for Fe, Zn, Mn, Cu, Pb, Cd, chloride, nitrate, sulfate, and phosphate to evaluate their suitability for human consumption. Overall, most measured parameters fell within World Health Organization guideline limits for drinking water, and cadmium and lead were below the analytical detection limits, indicating minimal contamination by these toxic metals. This project strengthened my interest in environmental and water-quality chemistry while providing useful baseline data for local water safety assessment.

research.title: Ligand Design
research.description: I design and study dirhodium-based complexes that drive selective chemical reactions and detect harmful organophosphate compounds. By fine‑tuning the ligands that surround these metal centers, my research advances both the creation of valuable chiral chemicals and the development of smart sensors for safer environments.

research.title: Catalysis and DFT conformational analysis
research.description: My research centers on developing heteroleptic dirhodium catalysts designed to enhance asymmetric chemical transformations. I use computational methods, including density functional theory (DFT), to analyze how different ligand conformations influence catalytic performance, guiding the creation of more efficient and selective catalytic systems.

research.title: Computational Chemistry
research.description: My research integrates computational modeling with experimental chemistry to understand and predict chemical reactivity. By interpreting experimental results through theoretical insights, I identify key factors that control reaction outcomes and use this knowledge to design more effective catalysts for selective transformations.

research.title: Molecular Sensing
research.description: My work focuses on designing transition metal–based chemical probes for the selective detection of biologically relevant molecules. By tuning metal–ligand interactions and electronic properties, I aim to create responsive systems that can recognize and signal the presence of specific biomolecules, advancing applications in chemical sensing, diagnostics, and environmental monitoring.
